puzzles.title: Copying a struct
puzzles.question: What does this print?
puzzles.explanation: Structs are value types. `var b = a` copies the value, so mutating `b` cannot affect `a`. Had `P` been a class, both names would point at the same instance and the answer would be 5.
whyOthersWrong: That would be true for a reference type (class), not a struct.
`x` has a default value and is never optional.
The code is valid Swift; `a` and `b` are both `var`.

puzzles.title: Protocol extension dispatch
puzzles.question: What does this print?
puzzles.explanation: `f()` is not a requirement of protocol `G`, it only exists in the extension. Calls through the existential type `G` are statically dispatched to the extension's implementation, so `S.f()` never runs. Adding `func f()` to the protocol body would make it a requirement and print B.
whyOthersWrong: B would require `f()` to be declared inside `protocol G`, enabling dynamic dispatch.
Only one implementation is called.
The code compiles; shadowing an extension method is legal.

puzzles.title: defer and the return value
puzzles.question: What does this print?
puzzles.explanation: The return value is copied before the `defer` block runs. `defer` executes as the scope exits, mutating the local `x` after its value has already been handed back. With an `inout` parameter or a reference type the mutation would be observable.
whyOthersWrong: The increment happens after the value is captured for return.
`defer` runs exactly once.
`defer` inside a function body is valid.

puzzles.title: mutating on a let value
puzzles.question: What happens here?
puzzles.explanation: A `mutating` method may only be called on a mutable value. `s` is a `let`, so the compiler rejects the call before the program ever runs. Changing `let` to `var` fixes it.
whyOthersWrong: Nothing is printed; the code does not compile.
Nothing is printed; the code does not compile.
This is caught at compile time, not at runtime.

puzzles.title: Type of an optional chain
puzzles.question: What is the type of `r`?
puzzles.explanation: Optional chaining always wraps the result in an optional, because the whole expression evaluates to nil when the base is nil. Even though `b` is a non-optional `Int`, `a?.b` is `Int?`.
whyOthersWrong: Chaining adds a level of optionality; it never returns a plain value.
`r` holds the property, not the containing value.
Swift infers a concrete type here, not `Any`.

puzzles.title: Breaking a closure retain cycle
puzzles.question: Which one breaks a strong reference cycle between an object and its stored closure?
puzzles.explanation: A capture list such as `[weak self]` (or `[unowned self]`) stops the closure from holding a strong reference back to the object, so ARC can deallocate it. The other keywords change escaping semantics, initialization timing or inheritance, none of which affect ownership.
whyOthersWrong: `@escaping` only tells the compiler the closure may outlive the call; it makes cycles more likely, not less.
`lazy` delays initialization; ownership is unchanged.
`final` prevents subclassing and can enable static dispatch; it has no effect on retain counts.

puzzles.title: When does lazy run?
puzzles.question: What is printed first?
puzzles.explanation: A `lazy var` initializer does not run until the property is first read. Creating `C()` prints nothing, so "made" comes first, then "init" when `c.v` is accessed, then "1".
whyOthersWrong: The initializer is deferred until the first access to `v`.
The value is printed last, after its initializer runs.
All three lines are printed.

puzzles.title: Actors and await
puzzles.question: What can happen at an `await` inside an actor method?
puzzles.explanation: Swift actors are reentrant. Suspending at an `await` releases the actor, so another queued call can enter and mutate state. Any assumption you made about the actor's state before the suspension point must be re-checked afterwards.
whyOthersWrong: The actor is not held across suspension points; state can change.
Reentrancy exists precisely to avoid deadlocks.
Execution resumes after the await, it does not start over.

puzzles.title: Counting characters
puzzles.question: What does this print?
puzzles.explanation: Swift's `Character` is an extended grapheme cluster. "e" followed by U+0301 (combining acute accent) renders as a single user-perceived character "é", so `count` is 1. `s.unicodeScalars.count` would be 2 and `s.utf8.count` would be 3.
whyOthersWrong: That is the number of Unicode scalars, not characters.
That is the UTF-8 byte count.
The string is not empty.

puzzles.title: Iterating a Dictionary
puzzles.question: What is the iteration order of a Swift Dictionary?
puzzles.explanation: Dictionary is an unordered collection; its iteration order is an implementation detail and can even differ between runs because of hash seeding. Sort explicitly (`dict.sorted { $0.key < $1.key }`) whenever order matters — especially before rendering a list.
whyOthersWrong: That is the behaviour of an array of pairs or an ordered dictionary type.
Keys are hashed, not sorted.
Values do not influence storage order.

puzzles.title: Cost of binary search
puzzles.question: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array?
puzzles.explanation: Each comparison discards half of the remaining range, so the number of steps is the number of times n can be halved: log2(n). The array must already be sorted; sorting it first would cost O(n log n) and dominate.
whyOthersWrong: Constant time would mean the answer is found without depending on the size at all.
Scanning every element is linear search, which is what binary search improves on.
That is the cost of sorting the array, not of searching it.

puzzles.title: Appending to an Array
puzzles.question: What is the amortised cost of appending one element to a Swift Array?
puzzles.explanation: Array over-allocates capacity and doubles it when full. Most appends write into spare capacity in constant time; the occasional reallocation copies n elements, but spread over all the appends that cost averages out to O(1) per append.
whyOthersWrong: Nothing is being halved or searched here.
A single reallocation is O(n), but that is the worst case, not the amortised one.
That is a sorting cost, unrelated to appending.

puzzles.title: Dictionary lookup cost
puzzles.question: What is the average time complexity of looking a key up in a Dictionary?
puzzles.explanation: A dictionary hashes the key to find its bucket directly, so an average lookup does not depend on how many entries exist. With pathological hash collisions it degrades towards O(n), which is why a good Hashable implementation matters.
whyOthersWrong: That is the cost of searching a balanced tree, not a hash table.
Only in the degenerate case where every key collides into one bucket.
Dictionaries are unordered; insertion order does not affect lookup cost.

puzzles.title: Inserting at the front
puzzles.question: What does inserting an element at index 0 of an Array cost?
puzzles.explanation: Array stores its elements contiguously, so making room at the front means shifting every existing element one slot to the right. When you need cheap insertion at both ends, reach for a deque instead of an array.
whyOthersWrong: Only appending at the end is constant time.
No halving happens; every element moves.
One insertion is linear; you would need n insertions to reach quadratic.

puzzles.title: Cost of sorting
puzzles.question: What is the worst-case complexity of Swift's sort() on an array?
puzzles.explanation: Swift uses an introsort-style hybrid whose worst case is O(n log n). That bound is why quicksort alone is not used: its worst case is quadratic, so the standard library falls back to heapsort when recursion runs too deep.
whyOthersWrong: No comparison sort can beat n log n in the general case.
That is naive quicksort's worst case, which the standard library avoids.
Sorting must at least look at every element.

puzzles.title: Is sort() stable?
puzzles.question: Does Swift guarantee that sort() keeps equal elements in their original order?
puzzles.explanation: Swift's sort is documented as not guaranteed stable, even though the current implementation happens to be. Relying on it is a bug waiting for a standard library update. When order among equals matters, sort by an explicit tie-breaking key.
whyOthersWrong: Stability is explicitly not promised by the documentation.
Value semantics have nothing to do with sort stability.
The size of the input does not change what is guaranteed.

puzzles.title: Array contains vs Set contains
puzzles.question: Why is Set.contains usually faster than Array.contains for large collections?
puzzles.explanation: A set hashes the value and jumps straight to the right bucket, giving an average O(1) test. An array has no such index, so it compares elements one by one until it finds a match, which is O(n).
whyOthersWrong: Sets are unordered; being sorted is not how they find elements.
No caching is involved; each lookup is computed afresh.
A hash table usually uses more memory, not less, in exchange for speed.

puzzles.title: Finding a pair that sums to a target
puzzles.question: What is the best average complexity for finding two numbers that add to a target?
puzzles.explanation: One pass storing each seen value in a dictionary lets you ask whether target minus the current value has already appeared. Each lookup is average O(1), so the whole scan is O(n), at the cost of O(n) extra memory.
whyOthersWrong: Sorting first and using two pointers works, but the sort dominates at n log n.
That is the brute force of comparing every pair.
Every element has to be examined at least once.

puzzles.title: Why memoise Fibonacci?
puzzles.question: What does memoising a naive recursive Fibonacci change its complexity to?
puzzles.explanation: The naive recursion recomputes the same subproblems over and over, branching twice per call. Caching each result means every value from 0 to n is computed exactly once, turning exponential work into linear work plus O(n) memory.
whyOthersWrong: A single cached call is constant, but computing fib(n) still needs every smaller value.
Memoisation removes work; it never introduces a logarithmic factor.
The whole point is that the repeated subproblems disappear.

puzzles.title: Indexing a linked list
puzzles.question: What does reaching the n-th element of a singly linked list cost?
puzzles.explanation: A linked list has no contiguous storage to offset into, so reaching a position means following one pointer at a time from the head. That is the trade for cheap insertion and removal once you already hold a node.
whyOthersWrong: Constant-time indexing needs contiguous storage, which is what an array has.
There is no halving to exploit; the nodes are not ordered by address.
Nothing is being sorted.

puzzles.title: Stack versus queue
puzzles.question: Which order does a stack use?
puzzles.explanation: A stack removes the most recently added element first, which is exactly what a call stack or an undo history needs. A queue is the other way round: first in, first out, as in a print spool or a task pipeline.
whyOthersWrong: That describes a queue.
Neither structure sorts its contents.
Both have a strictly defined order.

puzzles.title: Visiting a tree level by level
puzzles.question: Which structure gives you a level-by-level traversal of a tree?
puzzles.explanation: Breadth-first traversal enqueues the children of each node and processes them in arrival order, so a whole level is visited before the next begins. Swapping the queue for a stack turns the same code into a depth-first traversal.
whyOthersWrong: A stack gives depth-first order, diving down one branch first.
A set has no order, so it cannot drive a traversal.
A dictionary maps keys to values; it does not sequence the visit.

puzzles.title: Quicksort's bad day
puzzles.question: When does quicksort degrade to quadratic time?
puzzles.explanation: If the pivot is always the smallest or largest remaining element, each partition peels off one element and recursion depth becomes n. Naive first-element pivots do exactly that on already sorted data, which is why real implementations randomise or use the median of three.
whyOthersWrong: Random input is the case quicksort handles well, averaging n log n.
Short inputs are fast regardless of the algorithm.
Duplicates hurt some partition schemes but are not the classic worst case.

puzzles.title: In-place or not
puzzles.question: What does it mean for an algorithm to run in place?
puzzles.explanation: In place means the extra memory used does not grow with the input, beyond a constant number of variables. It says nothing about speed: an in-place algorithm can be slower than one that buys time with a large auxiliary buffer.
whyOthersWrong: Individual elements are still swapped and copied; only the extra allocation is bounded.
Threading is a separate concern entirely.
Using less memory does not imply using less time.

puzzles.title: A bad Hashable implementation
puzzles.question: What happens if hash(into:) always feeds the same constant?
puzzles.explanation: Every value lands in the same bucket, so the dictionary degenerates into a linear scan through a collision chain. It stays correct because equality still decides matches, but the performance guarantee is gone. Hash quality is a performance contract, not a correctness one.
whyOthersWrong: Correctness survives, but lookup cost changes dramatically.
A poor hash is legal; it is slow, not fatal.
Equality is defined separately by ==, and is unaffected.

puzzles.title: first(where:) versus filter
puzzles.question: Why prefer first(where:) over filter { }.first?
puzzles.explanation: first(where:) returns as soon as an element matches, while filter walks the entire collection and builds a new array only to discard all but one element. On a large collection that is wasted time and wasted allocation.
whyOthersWrong: Laziness is a separate feature reached through the lazy property.
Neither call sorts anything.
Both hand back an optional, because there may be no match.

puzzles.title: reduce versus reduce(into:)
puzzles.question: Why is reduce(into:) preferred when accumulating into an array or dictionary?
puzzles.explanation: Plain reduce passes the accumulator by value and returns a new one each step, which can copy the whole collection on every element. reduce(into:) mutates one accumulator in place, so building a dictionary from n items stays linear instead of quadratic.
whyOthersWrong: Neither form runs concurrently.
Both are eager; laziness comes from the lazy view.
Both visit elements in the same order.

puzzles.title: Subscripting a String
puzzles.question: What does this code do?
puzzles.explanation: String is not indexed by Int, because characters are variable-width grapheme clusters and a numeric offset would not be a constant-time position. You need String.Index, for example s[s.index(s.startIndex, offsetBy: 2)].
whyOthersWrong: Nothing is printed; the code does not compile.
It would return a Character only if an Int subscript existed, which it does not.
The compiler rejects it before the program can run.

puzzles.title: Creating an enum from a raw value
puzzles.question: What is the type of `d`?
puzzles.explanation: The raw value initialiser is failable: the string might not match any case, so it returns an optional. Only the plain case reference, such as Suit.hearts, gives you a non-optional value.
whyOthersWrong: That would require the initialiser to be non-failable.
The raw value is the input, not the result.
Never is the uninhabited type, returned by functions that do not return.

puzzles.title: What guard let unwraps into
puzzles.question: Where is a value bound by guard let available?
puzzles.explanation: guard binds the unwrapped value in the enclosing scope, so it stays available for the rest of the function. That is the difference from if let, whose binding lives only inside the if body, and it is why guard suits early returns.
whyOthersWrong: The else block runs when the unwrap failed, so there is nothing to use there.
The binding outlives its own line; that is the whole point.
It is very much in scope afterwards.

puzzles.title: Making a widget button work
puzzles.question: How does a button inside a widget perform an action without opening the app?
puzzles.explanation: Widgets are rendered by a separate process from archived views, so there is no live code to run a closure. Interactive widgets on iOS 17 and later use Button(intent:) with an AppIntent, which the system executes on your behalf.
whyOthersWrong: A closure would need the view's code to still be alive, which it is not.
Widgets have no delegate callbacks for user taps.
It works from iOS 17 onwards, through App Intents.

puzzles.title: Sharing data with a widget
puzzles.question: How does an app share stored data with its widget extension?
puzzles.explanation: The app and its extension are separate processes with separate sandboxes. An App Group grants both a shared container directory, which is the only supported way to put a file or a UserDefaults suite where both can reach it.
whyOthersWrong: A singleton lives in one process's memory; the extension has its own copy.
Static state is per process too, for the same reason.
NotificationCenter does not cross process boundaries.

reference.title: Sharing data with your containing app

puzzles.title: Why a widget stops updating
puzzles.question: Why might a widget stop refreshing as often as its timeline asks?
puzzles.explanation: WidgetKit gives each widget a daily refresh budget based on how the user actually engages with it. Asking for frequent entries does not guarantee them, so timelines should stay cheap and reload only when something meaningful changed.
whyOthersWrong: A leak would show as a crash or termination, not as throttling.
Storage pressure does not govern refresh scheduling.
Appearance has nothing to do with the refresh budget.

reference.title: WidgetKit — Keeping a widget up to date

puzzles.title: Refreshing a widget after a change
puzzles.question: What do you call after writing new data so the widget redraws?
puzzles.explanation: WidgetCenter.shared.reloadTimelines(ofKind:) asks the system to rebuild that widget's timeline. Reloading a single kind is preferred over reloadAllTimelines, because every reload draws from the same limited refresh budget.
whyOthersWrong: setNeedsDisplay is a UIKit call inside one process; widgets are archived remotely.
objectWillChange drives SwiftUI inside a live app, not an extension's timeline.
viewDidLoad is a UIViewController lifecycle method.

puzzles.title: What a timeline holds
puzzles.question: What does a WidgetKit timeline consist of?
puzzles.explanation: A timeline is a list of entries, each carrying a date and the data to show from that moment, plus a policy for when to ask for more. The system renders the right entry as its date arrives without waking your extension again.
whyOthersWrong: The reload policy hints at timing, but the timeline itself carries entries.
Views are built from an entry; they are not what the timeline stores.
Widgets do not run background tasks of their own.

puzzles.title: Control Center controls
puzzles.question: Which iOS version introduced ControlWidget for Control Center?
puzzles.explanation: ControlWidget arrived in iOS 18, letting apps ship buttons and toggles into Control Center and the Lock Screen. Interactive home screen widgets came one release earlier, in iOS 17, which is a common source of confusion.
whyOthersWrong: iOS 16 brought Lock Screen widgets, not Control Center controls.
iOS 17 brought interactive widgets and StandBy.
iOS 15 predates all of this.

puzzles.title: Lock Screen widget families
puzzles.question: Which widget family renders as a rectangle on the Lock Screen?
puzzles.explanation: The accessory families are the Lock Screen ones: accessoryRectangular, accessoryCircular and accessoryInline. The system families are for the Home Screen. Accessory widgets are also rendered with a vibrant, largely monochrome treatment.
whyOthersWrong: systemSmall is a Home Screen family.
systemMedium is the wider Home Screen family.
That one is the small circular gauge, not a rectangle.

puzzles.title: Exposing an action to Siri
puzzles.question: What makes an App Intent available as a Siri phrase without user setup?
puzzles.explanation: Conforming a type to AppShortcutsProvider declares shortcuts with spoken phrases that are available as soon as the app is installed. Plain App Intents still work in the Shortcuts app, but the user has to build the shortcut themselves.
whyOthersWrong: No plist key registers an intent phrase.
URL schemes open the app; they do not create Siri phrases.
Spotlight surfaces content in search, not spoken shortcuts.

puzzles.title: Making content searchable
puzzles.question: Which framework indexes app content for the system search field?
puzzles.explanation: CoreSpotlight lets an app donate CSSearchableItem records so its content appears in system search. Tapping a result launches the app with the item identifier, which you use to navigate straight to that content.
whyOthersWrong: CoreData is persistence; it does not index for system search.
CoreServices is a broad low-level framework, not the search index API.
SearchKit is an older macOS text indexing API.

puzzles.title: Local notifications and permission
puzzles.question: Does scheduling a local notification require the user's permission?
puzzles.explanation: Local and remote notifications both need authorisation through UNUserNotificationCenter. Without it, a scheduled request is accepted but nothing is presented to the user, which makes the failure easy to miss during development.
whyOthersWrong: Being local does not exempt it from authorisation.
Sound is one of the options you request, not what triggers the requirement.
The requirement holds regardless of app state.

puzzles.title: What the deployment target means
puzzles.question: What does the iOS deployment target setting control?
puzzles.explanation: The deployment target is the earliest OS version the app will install and run on. The SDK you build against is separate and is usually newer, which is why newer APIs need an availability check to stay usable on older systems.
whyOthersWrong: That is the base SDK, chosen by the Xcode version.
Simulators are limited by the installed runtimes, not by this setting.
The Swift language version is its own build setting.

puzzles.title: Using a newer API safely
puzzles.question: How do you call an iOS 18 API in an app that also supports iOS 17?
puzzles.explanation: if #available(iOS 18, *) asks the runtime whether the API exists and lets you provide a fallback. The compiler enforces this: calling a newer symbol without a check, or without an @available annotation, is a build error.
whyOthersWrong: try? handles thrown errors, not missing symbols.
@objc concerns Objective-C interoperability.
Optional chaining is about nil values, not API availability.

puzzles.title: Writing next to your resources
puzzles.question: Can an app write files into its own app bundle at runtime?
puzzles.explanation: The bundle is signed and mounted read-only; writing there would invalidate the signature. Runtime data belongs in the container directories instead, typically Documents for user data and Caches or Application Support for regenerable files.
whyOthersWrong: The signature makes this impossible on device.
Build configuration does not change the sandbox rules.
Size is irrelevant; the location is what is forbidden.

puzzles.title: UserDefaults across an extension
puzzles.question: Which UserDefaults does an extension share with its app?
puzzles.explanation: UserDefaults(suiteName:) with the App Group identifier gives both processes the same store. UserDefaults.standard is per sandbox, so the app and the extension each get their own and silently disagree.
whyOthersWrong: standard is not shared across the sandbox boundary.
Keychain groups share credentials, not defaults.
Sharing is possible through the App Group suite.

puzzles.title: What survives a reinstall
puzzles.question: Which store can outlive deleting and reinstalling an app?
puzzles.explanation: Keychain items can persist after an app is deleted, which is why credentials sometimes reappear on reinstall. Everything inside the app container, defaults included, is removed with the app. Treat this as a real behaviour to handle, not a feature to rely on.
whyOthersWrong: Defaults live in the container and go with it.
The Documents directory is part of the container.
Caches can be purged even while the app is installed.

puzzles.title: Why write atomically
puzzles.question: What does Data.write with the atomic option protect against?
puzzles.explanation: An atomic write goes to a temporary file first and is then moved into place in one step. If the process is killed midway, the old file survives intact instead of leaving a half-written one, which matters when two processes share a container.
whyOthersWrong: It orders nothing between threads; that needs actual synchronisation.
Encryption is governed by file protection classes.
It is slightly slower, not faster.

puzzles.title: Where UI updates belong
puzzles.question: On which thread must UIKit and SwiftUI views be updated?
puzzles.explanation: UI work must happen on the main thread. Swift Concurrency expresses this with the @MainActor annotation, which the compiler checks, replacing the older habit of remembering to hop to DispatchQueue.main by hand.
whyOthersWrong: Touching views off the main thread causes unpredictable failures.
Background queues are for work that does not touch the UI.
The render server is internal and not somewhere you dispatch to.

puzzles.title: Text that respects the user's size
puzzles.question: What makes text scale with the user's preferred content size?
puzzles.explanation: Semantic text styles such as .body or .headline carry Dynamic Type scaling, so text follows the size the user chose in Settings. A hard-coded point size ignores that entirely and is a common accessibility failure.
whyOthersWrong: A fixed size is exactly what does not scale.
A custom font still needs a scaling metric to participate.
Constraining height fights the scaling rather than enabling it.

puzzles.title: What a typealias creates
puzzles.question: Does a typealias create a new, distinct type?
puzzles.explanation: A typealias is only another spelling for an existing type, so the two are interchangeable everywhere. When you want the compiler to keep two things apart, such as a UserID and an OrderID, wrap the value in a struct instead.
whyOthersWrong: No new type is introduced, so no type safety is gained.
The behaviour is the same whatever kind of type is aliased.
Protocol aliases behave the same way.

puzzles.title: When an Array actually copies
puzzles.question: What does this print?
puzzles.codeSnippet:
var a = [1, 2, 3]
var b = a
b.append(4)
print(a.count, b.count)
puzzles.explanation: Array has value semantics implemented with copy on write: assigning shares the buffer, and the copy happens only when one side mutates while the buffer is shared. So b grows to four elements while a still has three.
whyOthersWrong: That would be reference semantics, which arrays do not have.
The append did happen, so b must be longer.
The code is valid Swift.
